items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: In October 1955, I played a two days jazz festival in Lyon which featured Sydney Bechet, Chet Baker and myself.

ctx.x: We arrived back in Paris the 24th of August. I started working at the Trois Maillets the 15th of September and my sister left for the U.S.A. the 16th.

I had the privilege of going out of the club now and then to do ates in different places and that was the way I worked until February of 1956. In October 1955, I played a two days jazz festival in Lyon which featured Sydney Bechet, Chet Baker and myself. Sidney was the main attraction because his popularity had grown immensely since 1950 and he was the biggest crowd drawing jazz musician in Europe. At one time, I didn't dig him mostly I suppose because I didn't like the sound of soprano saxophone. But I dug him…

The musicians that accompanied me at the Trois Maillets were Michel de Villers, whom I had made my first tour with as a member of the Edouard's band. He was now playing alto and baritone sax. The pianist was Andre Persiany who was known as the French Milt Buckner. We called him Pepe. My friend Guy Lafitte was on tenor. items.q: We knew each other casually, but eventually got better acquainted

ctx.x: One night the orchestra of Noble Sissle who was working in a big white hotel was engaged at the Arcadia to play a battle of jazz between Russell and the other white orchestra whose name I don't remember. I had seen Sissle on stage when I was in Cincinnati and in my estimation he was pretty much a ham actor. So it was a night that we were looking forward to, and the Uncle Tom in him was really shown when his band came in dressed in red frocktail coats which made them look like a circus monkey band. There were some…

trombonist and Sidney Bechet who was supposed to be the jazz man of the band, but I was never a lover of the soprano sax so Bechet didn't tell me anything. The band as a whole was the most jazzless negro orchestra I had ever heard. The white band made Sissle's sound like a fifth-grade school band and Russel's orchestra made Sissles sound like it was the first time they had ever played musical instruments. It has been said that a band is no better than its leader and I felt sorry for the musicians because they had…

We went to Philadelphia to play one week at the Earl Theater and that was the hardest week I ever worked in a theater. Paul Barbarin left Russel then and went back to New Orleans. He was replaced by James Smith who became a good buddy of mine.
